title: Sound before meaning
hook: Japji is meant to be heard; we will listen to each pauri before we learn what it says

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gurmukhi, the script from the Guru's mouth. Your line was read with the mouth first. Did you find a Gurmukhi letter out in the world and say it? Day one hundred fifty-eight.

A lullaby in a language you don't speak can still get through. So can a chant in a stadium, or a hymn at a wedding where you catch maybe one word in ten. The meaning never arrives. The sound does, and it stays. Japji often reaches people that way first. In homes where it's recited at dawn, children hear it drifting from a kitchen or a car radio long before anyone explains what it says.
screen: `A SONG YOU DON'T UNDERSTAND.` → `THE SOUND STAYED.` → `JAPJI AT DAWN, FROM THE KITCHEN.`

segments.voice: So this camp has a rule. Almost every pauri, every stanza, gets two days. The first day is sound: we listen, and say the opening line out loud. The second day is meaning: what the Guru is saying. Sound first, then meaning. Why that order? Partly because of what Japji is. The name comes from jap, to recite, to repeat. It was made to be said, not only studied. It's the first bani of the morning Nitnem, and it's often said from memory. It has thirty-eight pauris, with a short salok at the start and another at the end, and a steady recitation fits into an ordinary morning. Partly it's because of how Gurbani, the Guru's word, speaks about itself. The hymns keep praising the shabad, the word as sound, and the naad, the sound that moves through everything, as things that work on the one who hears them. Japji itself will give four whole pauris to one word: suniai, by listening. We'll get there. And partly it's simply how learning works. Understanding goes deeper when it lands on something already familiar. If you've said a line thirty times, then on the day its meaning arrives, it has somewhere to sit. There's a humility in it, too. You don't have to understand everything before you start. You're allowed to listen first. And if you grew up Sikh and can't read Gurmukhi, or follow only some of the Punjabi in the hymns, you're in large company, especially far from Punjab. Some people carry a quiet embarrassment about that. There's no need. The Granth's language is centuries old, fluent speakers look words up too, and this camp is built for exactly where you are. When we do open the meanings, we'll follow Macauliffe's 1909 translation, retold in plain words. But for now, the instruction is short. Listen.
screen: `TWO DAYS FOR EACH PAURI.` · `JAPJI IS MADE TO BE SAID.` · `THE SHABAD WORKS ON THE LISTENER.` · `LISTEN FIRST, UNDERSTAND LATER.` · then, large: `SOUND BEFORE MEANING.`

segments.voice: Today's practice starts now and finishes later. Now: close your eyes, and just listen to whatever is around you, the hum of a fridge, traffic, a bird, your own breath. Don't name the sounds. Just hear them. Later today, find a recording of Japji Sahib, there are many, and let it play once, all the way through, while you cook or drive or walk. Don't follow the words. Don't look anything up. Let it wash past. If you pray, you can simply sit inside it. The bell holds the time.
Japji Sahib. In this camp, each pauri of it is heard and said before it is explained, sound before meaning.
Your line: listen before you understand. Play Japji once today, start to finish, and notice one sound that stays with you afterward. Day one hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: Sikhs recite or listen to Japji Sahib each morning, often from memory, as the first bani of Nitnem; children often hear it long before they study its meaning.

original.note: Gurmukhi: Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak's morning hymn; ji and sahib add respect.

trapdoor: what you thought: learn what it means, then say it.
what it means: say it and hear it first, so the meaning has somewhere to land.
what a scholar hears: Gurbani praises shabad and naad, the word as sound; Japji itself gives four pauris to suniai, listening.

sources.ref: Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), vol. 1, the Japji

notes: Japji: thirty-eight pauris plus opening and closing saloks; about twenty minutes to recite at a steady pace. Confirm.
'Almost every pauri gets two days': the outline gives pauris 9–11 and some later pauris one day each. Wording hedged with 'almost'.
The four suniai pauris are 8–11. Confirm.
Review (2026-10-01): hook no longer opens 'Think of'; 'most Sikh children', 'many Sikhs' and the unsourced 'around twenty minutes' removed or softened (also in the myth reveal and howItsDone).
